qa_pairs.question: Compile authoritative RESIDENTIAL bathroom and kitchen planning standards with specific METRIC clearances and their sources. Cover in detail: (1) BATHROOM fixture-to-fixture spacing — minimum clear distance between basin and WC, WC and shower/tub, basin and basin, and the clear floor space in front of each of WC, basin, shower and tub; (2) WET/DRY zoning — the recommended separation of wet zones (shower, tub) from dry zones (basin, WC, storage) in a residential bathroom; (3) fixture ORDERING by frequency of use — best practice for placing the most-used fixtures (basin) nearer the entry and less-used (WC, shower) deeper; (4) KITCHEN work-triangle — the recommended minimum and maximum length of each leg (sink-cooktop-refrigerator) and the total triangle perimeter, plus minimum aisle/walkway widths between opposing counters. Prioritize NKBA Kitchen & Bath planning guidelines (the 31 bathroom / 41 kitchen guidelines), Neufert 'Architects Data', and Panero & Zelnik. For every value give the metric number, the context, and the source.
qa_pairs.answer:
**1. Bathroom Fixture-to-Fixture Spacing and Clearances**
Designing a residential bathroom requires adherence to ergonomic clearances to prevent physical collisions, maximize accessibility, and meet building codes. The standards governing these spaces are primarily defined by fixture centerlines, edge gaps, and clear floor spaces.

*   **Basin and Water Closet (WC) Spacing:**
    *   To provide adequate elbow clearance for grooming, the National Kitchen and Bath Association (NKBA) recommends that the centerline of the basin maintain a minimum distance of **508 mm** from the WC or any adjacent sidewall [1], [2]. Building codes enforce a strict minimum of **381 mm** [1], [2].
    *   Neufert’s standards suggest setting the WC centerline at **400 mm** from any side obstacle [2]. 
    *   Panero and Zelnik approach this via a lateral clear zone, recommending a minimum separation of **300 mm** from the outer edge of the toilet to an adjacent vanity cabinet [3], [2].
*   **WC and Shower/Tub Spacing:** 
    *   The NKBA recommends a centerline-to-barrier clearance of at least **457 mm** from the WC to a shower enclosure or bathtub, while statutory codes allow a reduced minimum of **381 mm** [4], [2]. 
    *   Neufert recommends **400 mm** to support natural seated postures [4], [2]. 
    *   To prevent interference when exiting the bath, Panero and Zelnik require a minimum lateral separation of **300 mm** from the outer edge of the toilet bowl to the entry plane of the shower [5].
*   **Basin-to-Basin Spacing (Double Vanity):** 
    *   The NKBA recommends a centerline-to-centerline distance of at least **914 mm** between two basins, whereas building codes permit a minimum of **762 mm** [5], [6], [2]. 
    *   Additionally, a minimum edge-to-edge separation of **102 mm** must be maintained between the physical edges of freestanding or wall-hung basins [6], [2].
*   **Clear Floor Space in Front of Fixtures:** 
    *   **WC:** The NKBA recommends a clear floor space of **762 mm** from the front lip of the toilet bowl, with a code minimum of **533 mm** [7], [2]. Neufert recommends **600 mm**, and Panero & Zelnik suggest an optimal forward clearance of **750 to 900 mm** to accommodate a user bending forward [7], [2].
    *   **Basin:** The NKBA recommends **762 mm** of frontal clearance, while the code minimum is **533 mm** [7], [2]. Neufert advises **700 mm**, and Panero & Zelnik recommend a space of **762 mm by 1219 mm** [2].
    *   **Shower:** The NKBA recommends **762 mm** of clear space in front of the shower opening, while building codes enforce a minimum of **610 mm** [7], [2]. Both Neufert and Panero & Zelnik recommend a space of **900 mm by 900 mm** [2].
    *   **Bathtub:** Clear floor space running the length of the tub must extend out at least **762 mm** under NKBA guidelines, with a code minimum of **533 mm** [7], [2]. Panero & Zelnik recommend **600 mm** [2].

**2. Wet/Dry Zoning**
Zoning in a bathroom partitions high-humidity areas from low-humidity grooming spaces to prevent moisture migration and structural rot [8].
*   **Wet Zones (Shower, Tub):** These areas must be hydraulically isolated from dry zones using physical barriers, such as tempered, low-iron glass partition panels [9]. For curbless, barrier-free showers, the floor must slope toward the drain at a minimum rate of **20.8 mm/m** (approx. 2%) to contain water [9]. Shower walls require a continuous waterproof material to a height of at least **1829 mm** above the finished shower floor, or at least **76 mm** above the showerhead rough-in [10].
*   **Dry Zones (Basin, WC, Storage):** Dry zone layout prioritizes protecting cabinetry from moisture and ensuring user safety [11]. Electrical receptacles must be Ground-Fault Circuit Interrupter (GFCI) protected and located within **914 mm** of the outer edge of each basin [12].

**3. Fixture Ordering by Frequency of Use**
Architectural best practices arrange bathroom fixtures based on their frequency of use, moving from the entry door to the deepest part of the room. This optimizes spatial flow, privacy, and plumbing dynamics [13].
*   **Washbasin (Primary Zone):** As the most frequently used fixture for short tasks, Neufert recommends placing the basin closest to the entry door for rapid access [13]. Plumbed furthest upstream, its smaller drain line provides a clean vertical air path that prevents downstream trap siphonage [14].
*   **WC (Intermediate Zone):** Representing medium-frequency use with a high need for privacy, the toilet should be positioned deeper in the room or shielded behind a partition, vanity cabinet, or door swing to keep it out of the direct line of sight [13].
*   **Shower and Bathtub (Deep Zone):** Used less frequently but for longer periods, bathing fixtures are sited at the deepest point of the layout [13]. This creates a quiet zone away from walkways and contains heat and high humidity near the back walls [13].

**4. Kitchen Work-Triangle and Clearances**
The kitchen "work triangle" ergonomically connects the three primary work zones: cold storage (refrigerator), prep/cleaning (sink), and cooking (cooktop/oven) [15].
*   **Work-Triangle Leg Lengths:** To prevent crowding or excessive walking, the NKBA requires each individual leg of the triangle to measure at least **1219 mm** and no more than **2743 mm** [16], [17]. Neufert’s standards align closely, recommending an optimal range of **1200 mm to 2700 mm** [16], [17].
*   **Total Triangle Perimeter:** The cumulative perimeter of the triangle must not exceed **7925 mm** under NKBA guidelines [16], [17]. Neufert specifies an optimal perimeter range of **3600 mm to 6600 mm**, with an absolute maximum of 8000 mm [16], [17]. Panero & Zelnik recommend a total perimeter between approximately **3962 mm and 7925 mm** (13 to 26 feet) [18], [17]. No leg should be blocked by an island or cabinet edge by more than **305 mm** [16].
*   **Aisle and Walkway Widths (Between Opposing Counters):**
    *   *Single-Cook Work Aisle:* The NKBA mandates a minimum aisle width of **1067 mm** between opposing countertops or appliances [19], [17]. Neufert establishes a comfortable baseline at **1060 mm** (within a 1000 to 1200 mm range), and Panero & Zelnik recommend **1050 to 1200 mm** [19], [17].
    *   *Multi-Cook Work Aisle:* When multiple people cook together, the NKBA requires a minimum aisle of **1219 mm**, which is echoed by Neufert’s **1200 mm** baseline [19], [17].
    *   *General Walkways:* For paths handling standard household foot traffic without interfering with the work triangle, the NKBA sets a minimum width of **914 mm** [19], [17]. Neufert recommends **900 mm**, and Panero & Zelnik suggest **1000 mm** [19], [17].
